The fourth-century quarters had residential and religious structures, including a basilica-style church in the Dakhla oasis. Archaeologists also found coins, pottery fragments and tools.

The ​birth of these endangered big cats – including an exceedingly rare white tiger – has revitalised a team of zoo workers, he said.

euronews.description: During the appeal trial, Le Pen denied that the National Rally had a system to embezzle European Parliament funds and said the party acted in "good faith."

euronews.description: The announcement comes after authorities across Europe were hunting for the woman suspected of planting a bomb in Monaco that wounded three people, including a Ukrainian-born tycoon and his teenaged son.

rfi.title: Appeal court upholds Le Pen conviction but opens door to 2027 presidential bid
rfi.description: The Paris Court of Appeal has upheld an embezzlement conviction against far-right leader Marine Le Pen for misusing EU funds, but it reduced the lower court's ban on her standing for public office, opening up the possibility that she could run in the 2027 presidential election.

rfi.title: Macron makes historic visit to Syria despite security concerns
rfi.description: French President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Damascus, becoming the first European head of state to visit Syria since Bashar al-Assad's regime fell in 2024.

rfi.title: Climate justice in Africa: floods, fossil fuels and the fightback
rfi.description: This week in Spotlight on Africa, we look at climate change, environmental justice and the challenges of adaptation. While Europe's heatwaves make headlines, temperatures are also climbing across Africa, with parts of the Sahel approaching 50°C. West Africa is also experiencing severe flooding caused by climate change. Yet Africa is also a source of innovation and solutions, as we'll be discussing today.

rfi.title: Macron condemns Paraguayan senator's racist remarks as Mbappé hits back
rfi.description: Kylian Mbappé condemned a Paraguayan senator on Monday for making racist comments about him following France's World Cup victory over Paraguay, calling her "despicable" and "not worthy" of her position.

rfi.title: EU warns France under-15 social media bill could breach European law
rfi.description: The European Commission has warned that a French bill that would ban children under the age of 15 from social media would infringe the European Union’s online content law by giving French regulators powers that go beyond the bloc’s legal framework.

rfi.title: NATO summit in Ankara tests unity as Ukraine war and Trump tensions loom
rfi.description: As NATO leaders gather in Ankara tomorrow, Tuesday, the alliance faces a stark test of unity, burden-sharing and strategic clarity, with the war in Ukraine, transatlantic tensions and Middle East instability all pressing heavily on the agenda.

rfi.description: Charles de Ketelaere scored twice as Belgium swept past the United States 4-1 on Monday night to reach the last eight at the World Cup.

rfi.description: European football's governing body Uefa on Monday lashed out at the decision of World Cup organisers Fifa to suspend the immediate one-match ban of the United States striker Folarin Balogun following the intervention of US President Donald Trump.

rfi.title: France's first diagnosed Ebola patient recovers after treatment
rfi.description: A French doctor who was the first-ever diagnosed case of Ebola in the country has made a full recovery and has been discharged from hospital.

rfi.title: Major wildfires burn in Southern France as early fire season hits Europe
rfi.description: Firefighters are fighting wildfires across southern France and other parts of Europe, and authorities are warning that this year’s fire season has started a month earlier than usual after early heatwaves in May and June left vegetation particularly dry and vulnerable.

rfi.title: Macron to become first Western European leader to visit post-Assad Syria
rfi.description: French President Emmanuel Macron ​will visit ‌Syria to discuss ways to ​strengthen bilateral ​relations and issues of ⁠mutual interest, ​the Syrian presidency has announced, in what would be the first visit by a Western European head of state since Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.

rfi.title: Merino's late strike takes Spain past Portugal into World Cup quarter-finals
rfi.description: Mikel Merino scored in second half stoppage time at the Dallas Stadium on Monday to send Spain past Portugal into the last eight at the 2026 World Cup and end the World Cup career of Portugal skipper Cristiano Ronaldo.

rfi.title: Rebels seize key town of Anéfis as they tighten grip on northern Mali
rfi.description: Tuareg separatists and al-Qaeda affiliates appear to have secured control of a key town in northern Mali following a coordinated offensive by the rebels over the weekend. The Malian army and Russian mercenaries have been holed up in the key camp of Anéfis after the rebels launched their offensive on Saturday.

rfi.title: Tour de France bans spectators from third stage as fire burns in French Pyrenees
rfi.description: Spectators have been banned from the third stage of the Tour de France cycling race through the Pyrenees Monday, which will be adapted as a forest fire burns the area.

rfi.title: Facing heavy security, Tanzania protesters fear repeat of election violence
rfi.description: Tanzanians planning to protest on Tuesday against government repression are facing a heavy police presence and warnings from authorities, which recalls the mass killings that followed last October's disputed election.

rfi.title: England survive Azteca thriller to set up last eight showdown with Norway
rfi.description: England moved into a last eight clash with Norway after they beat Mexico 3-2 in a whirlwind game for the ages at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City.

rfi.title: Haaland's late strikes take Norway past Brazil to last eight for first time
rfi.description: Erling Haaland scored twice in the last 11 minutes to sweep Norway past Brazil into the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time.

rfi.title: Summit host Turkey eyes major weapons deals with NATO allies
rfi.description: Next week's NATO Summit in Ankara is expected to showcase Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s rising influence within the alliance, as he aims to use the gathering to overcome resistance to crucial arms deals and highlight the rapid growth of Turkey’s defence industry.

lemonde.title: EN DIRECT, procès en appel de Marine Le Pen : « Le dossier n’a pas changé mais le contexte politique si, avec l’élection présidentielle toute proche »
lemonde.description: La cheffe de file des députés du RN a été reconnue coupable et devra purger un an de prison ferme sous bracelet électronique. La cour d’appel de Paris a par ailleurs considéré que la peine d’inéligibilité qu’elle a prononcé avait été purgée. Tous ses coprévenus ont été condamnés en appel. Notre journaliste Laura Motet répond à vos questions sur la décision rendue mardi.

lemonde.description: Beaucoup de pays européens apparaissent tiraillés entre le souci de contribuer à l’effort ukrainien, la préservation d’une part d’ambiguïté stratégique sur leurs coopérations industrielles de défense, et la crainte de voir émerger un nouveau concurrent.

lemonde.title: Baccalauréat 2026 : un taux de réussite provisoire de 85,5 %, selon le ministre de l’éducation nationale
lemonde.description: L’an dernier, le taux définitif était de 91,8 %, en hausse sur un an pour les voies générales (96,4 %) et technologique (90,9 %) et stable pour la voie professionnelle (83,4 %).

lemonde.title: Le gouvernement annonce 3 milliards d’euros d’économies supplémentaires pour l’Etat et la Sécurité sociale
lemonde.description: L’objectif de 5 % de déficit public en 2026 que s’est fixé le gouvernement est « difficile à atteindre », mais tout sera fait pour « s’en rapprocher au maximum », a déclaré mardi le ministre de l’économie, Roland Lescure, à l’issue d’un comité d’alerte des finances publiques à Bercy.

spiegel.description: In der Qualifikation zur Basketball-WM setzen viele Stars aus. Nicht so Dennis Schröder, der Deutschland zu zwei Titeln geführt hat. Für den NBA-Profi sind auch Spiele mit unbekannten Teamkollegen eine Ehre.

spiegel.title: WM 2026 heute: Das sollten Sie vor den Spielen am Abend und in der Nacht wissen
spiegel.description: Mohamed Salah gegen Lionel Messi – wer entscheidet das Duell der Altstars im Achtelfinale für sich? Und: Überspringt die Schweiz die nächste Hürde? Alles Wichtige zu den Partien des Tages erfahren Sie hier.

spiegel.title: Ralph Siegel: Schlager-Komponist liegt im künstlichen Koma
spiegel.description: Er brachte den Deutschen »Ein bisschen Frieden« und viele weitere Schlager-Hits. Nun liegt Ralph Siegel laut Familie im künstlichen Koma. Erst vor wenigen Monaten hatte der 80-Jährige über seine Zukunft gesprochen.

spiegel.title: Quiz des Tages beim SPIEGEL: 7 Fragen zum Allgemeinwissen pro Tag
spiegel.description: Jeden Tag gibt es sieben Fragen zu den wichtigsten Themengebieten des politisch-gesellschaftlichen Geschehens. Testen Sie hier Ihr Wissen!

spiegel.title: Start-ups: Zahl der Gründungen in Deutschland steigt auf Rekordwert
spiegel.description: Mehr als 3000 Start-ups in sechs Monaten: In Deutschland gibt es einen Gründungsrekord. Das liegt auch an der boomenden KI. Der Abstand zu den USA ist noch groß, hierzulande soll sich aber einiges ändern.

spiegel.title: Hummeln: Zunge raus, Kopfschütteln, Mund abwischen – Hummeln zeigen offenbar ganz genau, was ihnen schmeckt
spiegel.description: Zuckerwasser ruft Lippenlecken hervor, salzige oder bittere Lösungen eine ablehnende Reaktion: Forscher haben speisende Hummeln ganz genau beobachtet.

spiegel.title: Nürnberg: Mutmaßlicher Drogendealer soll zwei Mädchen vergewaltigt haben
spiegel.description: Ein Mann soll eine 15- und eine 18-Jährige unter Drogen gesetzt, ein anderer sie dann vergewaltigt haben: Zwei Verdächtige sind in Nürnberg festgenommen worden. Die mutmaßliche Tat soll zu einem größeren Komplex gehören.

spiegel.title: Deep Purple: Ian Gillan über »Splat!« und den Trotz gegen die Branche
spiegel.description: Es lautet »Splat!« Nach diesem Geräusch haben Deep Purple ihr 24. Studioalbum benannt. Auch sonst, sagt Sänger Ian Gillan, hätten sie sich nie daran gehalten, was Manager und Plattenfirmen so wollten.

spiegel.title: KI-Schauspielerin Tilly Norwood bald in erster Hauptrolle zu sehen
spiegel.description: Ihre Entwickler wollen sie zur nächsten Scarlett Johansson oder Natalie Portman machen. Ob es so weit kommt, ist ungewiss. Einen ersten Spielfilm mit der KI-generierten Tilly Norwood soll es nun aber geben.

spiegel.title: Frankreich: Marine Le Pen darf bei Präsidentschaftswahl antreten – aber nur mit Fußfessel
spiegel.description: Ein Berufungsgericht in Frankreich hat Rechtspopulistin Marine Le Pen zu einer dreijährigen Haftstrafe verurteilt. Zwei Jahre ‌wurden zur Bewährung ausgesetzt, die verbleibende Zeit muss sie eine Fußfessel tragen.

spiegel.title: Lakenheath: Soldat entblößt sich und entgeht Verfahren
spiegel.description: Ein mutmaßlicher Exhibitionist soll in Großbritannien von seinem Status als US-Soldat profitiert haben. Recherchen des »Guardian« zeigen, dass es sich um keinen Einzelfall handelt.

spiegel.title: Was sich bei den EU-Fluggastrechten ändert
spiegel.description: Die Reform der EU-Fluggastrechte fällt für Reisende besser aus als befürchtet: Bei verspäteten Flügen gibt es weiter bis zu 600 Euro Entschädigung. Ein Ärgernis bleibt jedoch.

spiegel.title: Bundesverfassungsgericht prüft umstrittenes bayerisches Polizeigesetz
spiegel.description: Verstößt Bayerns Polizeiaufgabengesetz gegen Grundrechte? Mit dieser Frage muss sich das Bundesverfassungsgericht in Karlsruhe beschäftigen. Unter anderem geht es um den möglichen Einsatz von Handgranaten.

spiegel.title: Nato-Gipfel in Ankara: Mitgliedstaaten kündigen Milliarden-Deal für Aufklärungsflugzeuge an
spiegel.description: Kurz vor dem Nato-Gipfel in Ankara kündigen mehrere Mitgliedsstaaten den Kauf neuer Aufklärungsflugzeuge an. Nachdem die USA aus dem Projekt ausgestiegen ist, dürfte Deutschland den größten Anteil zahlen.

spiegel.title: Bettwanzen im Wander-Urlaub: Alpenvereine bitten um Hilfe auf Berghütten
spiegel.description: Der Berg ruft, der Rücken juckt: In immer mehr Berghütten gibt es Probleme mit Wanzen. Drei deutschprachige Alpenvereine wollen jetzt gemeinsam gegen die Parasiten vorgehen – auch mit Plastiktüten.

observador.title: Aberta investigação contra senadora que insultou Mbappé
observador.description: Celeste Amarilla pode ser condenada a uma pena até um ano de prisão, mas mostrou-se arrependida pelas declarações. No entanto, pondera processar Mbappé por "violência de género".

observador.title: Adiós, Mundial. Adiós, Martínez. Jesus vem salvar a seleção?
observador.description: Foi o adeus humilhante de uma geração de ouro. Portugal sai do Mundial com um futebol "pobre" e "cinzento". Com Martínez de saída e Ronaldo em lágrimas, fica o retrato de uma equipa sem chama.

observador.title: Príncipe Harry perde caso contra grupo do Daily Mail
observador.description: O grupo de sete queixosos, que inclui o príncipe Harry, Elton John e Elizabeth Hurley, acusava a Associated Newspapers de práticas ilegais de recolha de informação. Para o tribunal, não há provas.

observador.title: Hugo Soares elogia Governo: "Temos feito das tripas coração"
observador.description: Secretário-geral do PSD encerrou jornadas parlamentares da AD com críticas duras ao Chega. Paulo Núncio considera que "poucos fizeram tanto pela causa comunista como Ventura".

observador.title: VW perde 1500 milhões de euros e abandona parceria com Bosch
observador.description: Há quatro anos, o Grupo VW aliou-se à Bosch para o desenvolvimento de condução autónoma. Agora prepara-se para deitar por terra a parceria e os 1500 milhões de euros que investiu.

observador.title: 14h. Marine Le Pen condenada a três anos de prisão
observador.description: A líder da extrema-direita francesa ainda pode candidatar-se às presidenciais de 2027. Ainda neste jornal, as intervenções nas jornadas parlamentares da AD. E o despiste de um autocarro no Cacém.

observador.title: População de La Guaira critica militares por pilhagem
observador.description: "Carregaram o que roubaram em carrinhas deles [do exército]", afirma sobrevivente dos sismos. Esta denúncia não é única e surgem vários vídeos de pessoas a garantir que alguns militares pilham casas.

observador.title: Açores aprovam pesar pelas vítimas dos sismos na Venezuela
observador.description: Luís Garcia lembrou que os sismos deixaram "milhares de pessoas desalojadas". Reconhece ainda que Açores estão sujeitos a sismos e outros fenómenos naturais.

observador.title: Cidadãos pela Beira Baixa contra aceleração de renováveis
observador.description: Cidadãos afirmam que apenas 7% do território nacional tem aptidão para aceleração e que nem todo o território pode ser substituído por "mares de painéis". Alertam ainda para a saúde pública.

observador.title: Hamas reitera compromisso com cessar-fogo mas critica Israel
observador.description: O compromisso do Hamas da transição de poder para o Comité Nacional para a Administração de Gaza mantém-se. Mas o grupo acusa Israel de "tentativas contínuas da ocupação" e de obstruir o acordo.

observador.title: MAI. "Território desorganizado" aumenta hectares ardidos
observador.description: Luís Neves afirma que o país tem tido dificuldades na organização do território devido ao direito de reserva da propriedade. São necessárias medidas para resolver estes problemas.

observador.title: Droga. 26 pessoas detidas em operação contra tráfico
observador.description: Rede operava em Aveiro, Arouca, Estarreja, Vale de Cambra, Albergaria-a-Velha, Oliveira de Azeméis, São João da Madeira, Vila Nova de Gaia e Porto. Têm forte capacidade logística, dizem autoridades.

observador.title: Irão suspende negociações até EUA parar com ameaças
observador.description: No plano diplomático, o Irão, pela voz do MNE, decide suspender as negociações. Uma decisão que surge depois de Donald Trump ter ameaçado que os EUA estão prontos para uma intervenção militar.

observador.title: 13h. Venezuela. Perto de 15 toneladas de ajuda
observador.description: O material deve chegar amanhã a território venezuelano, assim como equipamentos de apoio à remoção de escombros. Ainda neste jornal, o acidente junto à estação ferroviária do Cacém.

observador.title: Tribunal condena Le Pen mas deixa porta aberta a eleições
observador.description: Marine Le Pen poderá candidatar-se às presidenciais de 2027. A decisão foi conhecida esta terça-feira, após Le Pen apresentar um recurso da condenação proferida em março de 2025.

observador.title: Almada vai passar a ter uma ligação fluvial para Algés
observador.description: A ligação entre Trafaria e Lisboa será prolongada até Oeiras (Pedrouços/Algés) e terá lugar todos os dias da semana, num período experimental de seis meses.

observador.title: "Mais um milhão e PIB não muda? É um milhão a fazer o mesmo"
observador.description: Presidente da CIP critica "abertura de portas sem ter em conta as necessidades da economia". Paulo Macedo avisa que "a próxima década definirá se Portugal converge ou estagna".

observador.title: Declaração ambiental para mina na Gudiña é obrigatória
observador.description: Comissão Europeia alerta para obrigatoriedade da avaliação de impacte ambiental transfronteiriça, que ainda não foi feita, sobre a exploração de volfrâmico, na Gudiña, Espanha, perto de Vinhais.

Researchers at the Institute of Environment recently installed a series of 3D-printed seawall tiles designed and developed at FIU's Robotics and Digital Fabrication Lab.

phys-org.title: Hawaiʻi island spinner dolphins are producing fewer calves
phys-org.description: Unexpectedly low calf numbers within the spinner dolphin population off Hawaiʻi Island were revealed in a study led by scientists with the Marine Mammal Research Program (MMRP) at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, along with national and international collaborators. Their research, published in Endangered Species Research, determined that calves make up only about 9% of the population, a stark contrast to the 17% expected in a healthy, stable population, raising urgent concerns about the long-

phys-org.title: Scientists enable DNA synthesis using only temperature instead of chemical reagents
phys-org.description: "Complex chemical processes are essential for making DNA." This long-held assumption in the field of biotechnology has been overturned by a Korean research team. A KAIST research team has developed the world's first foundational technology that enables the synthesis of desired DNA using only temperature. Using this technology, the team also demonstrated a "DNA temperature black box" that records temperature changes during shipping without electricity.

phys-org.title: Metallic rutile oxides break the rules of cooling
phys-org.description: Physicists have long puzzled over a strange contradiction inside a family of minerals called rutile oxides. These materials all share the same crystal structure—but while some of them, like titanium dioxide, are firmly insulating, others, like ruthenium dioxide, conduct electricity like a metal. So far, physicists have had little idea of why this happens.

phys-org.title: New Horizons watches the solar wind as it slows down
phys-org.description: Where does the solar system end and interstellar space begin? That's a question scientists have been working to answer using spacecraft traveling beyond the sun's influence. A team of researchers from the Southwest Research Institute, led by Heather Elliott, is using the Solar Wind Around Pluto (SWAP) instrument aboard New Horizons to track the solar wind in the outer reaches of the solar system.

phys-org.title: Reinventing pediatric dental training in Singapore
phys-org.description: Managing pediatric dental patients can be stressful for dental students and inexperienced practitioners, particularly when communicating with fearful and uncooperative children. Previous studies found that dental students experience three times the stress levels of seasoned specialists.

phys-org.title: Birds' efficient red blood cells convert metabolic 'waste' into fuel for rapid recovery
phys-org.description: New research finds that birds can use lactate, often thought of as a metabolic waste product, as a cellular fuel that aids in rapid recovery from a harmful state that impairs oxygen delivery. Hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen to our tissues, naturally converts to methemoglobin, which limits the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

phys-org.title: Citizen science could grow beyond data collection under 10 proposed recommendations
phys-org.description: Citizen science is booming and could play a much greater role in tackling climate change, reef health, biodiversity and public health challenges by involving members of the public throughout the research process, according to a new study.

phys-org.title: JWST finds the most distant barred galaxy candidate in the early universe
phys-org.description: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have identified what may be the most distant barred spiral galaxy ever discovered, dating to a time less than 1.2 billion years after the Big Bang. The paper outlining its properties was posted to the arXiv preprint server on June 23.

phys-org.title: Isotopic signatures link hot spring magmatic water to the subducting Pacific Plate
phys-org.description: Water flowing from hot springs near volcanoes often contains a mixture of meteoric water that has percolated underground and a deeper component known as magmatic water. Researchers at the University of Tsukuba used numerical simulations and isotopic data to show that magmatic water in hot springs and volcanic gases around Kussharo Caldera, Hokkaido, originates from the subducting Pacific Plate, which descends from the Kuril Trench to a depth of 125 kilometers (78 miles). The paper is published i

phys-org.title: Cheetah chases inspire researchers to make a biologically accurate video game
phys-org.description: Movement data from wild predator–prey encounters and controlled human catch-tag games have been combined to create realistic simulations of high-intensity movement dynamics and energetics—before being transformed into a publicly accessible video game. This game uses a citizen science approach to data collection and is helping to further our understanding of the role of movement decision-making and fatigue in life-or-death encounters.

phys-org.title: Researchers break a fundamental rule to create a new concept: Heat that can be directed and 'programmed'
phys-org.description: Normally, a material absorbs and emits heat in a linked way: A surface that absorbs heat well at a certain wavelength and direction will also emit heat in the same way. This fundamental relationship, known as reciprocity, limits the ability to independently control heat absorption and heat emission.

phys-org.title: New research finds connection to place predicts hurricane response among US coastal residents
phys-org.description: For U.S. coastal residents, storm surge is among the deadliest hurricane hazards, causing catastrophic property damage and loss of life, and scientists expect tropical storms to grow more intense. During Hurricane Ian in 2022, storm surge accounted for 41 of the 66 direct deaths. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is now underway, and while NOAA expects below-normal activity, emergency managers caution that it only takes one storm to devastate a community.

phys-org.title: Bumblebees exposed to up to 7 times as much toxic metal as honeybees
phys-org.description: Bumblebees collect up to seven times the amount of toxic heavy metals as honeybees even when foraging in the same environment, new research from the University of Cambridge has found. Exposure to these metals can affect everything from their ability to forage for food to their ability to reproduce.

phys-org.title: Massive calving episode in Greenland may foreshadow more rapid ice sheet loss
phys-org.description: In November 2025, a study led by Adrien Wehrlé, a researcher in the Department of Geography at the University of Zürich, Switzerland, looked at the massive calving response of one of West Greenland's active glaciers, Sermeq Kujalleq in the Kangia icefjord (SKK), to the drainage of two surface lakes. Called supraglacial lakes, these are temporary meltwater ponds that form and accumulate in depressions or holes on the surface of glaciers and ice sheets.

phys-org.title: New beetle genus named after One Piece's Monkey D. Luffy, encompassing two new species
phys-org.description: A research team from the Natural History Museum of Denmark has published a compelling new study in insect taxonomy in the open-access journal ZooKeys, officially establishing a new genus of rove beetle: Luffy gen. nov. The inspiration for the name comes directly from Monkey D. Luffy, the iconic protagonist of the globally popular manga and anime One Piece.

phys-org.title: Why we need to consider city shapes to save energy, water, and the climate
phys-org.description: The world's future is in cities. It is estimated that by 2050, 7 out of 10 people will live in urban areas (although a recent CSH study suggests that the growth of large cities may be less dramatic than current projections indicate, it still points to continued and substantial urban growth).

new-sci.title: 5 graphs that show how heatwaves are getting more dangerous
new-sci.description: Longer-lasting hot spells and high temperatures at night are making it harder to cope, leading to thousands more deaths from extreme heat

new-sci.title: Ovary identity shift after menopause may contribute to inflammation
new-sci.description: We used to think post-menopausal ovaries sat inert in the body, but evidence from mice suggests they may instead turn into an organ with a role in inflammation

new-sci.title: Bumblebee facial movements give clues to their inner lives
new-sci.description: A series of experiments shows that bees respond differently to tastes depending on their internal states, hinting that they have something akin to our emotions

new-sci.title: Artefacts hint at cultural exchange between Neanderthals and humans
new-sci.description: A cave on the Turkish Mediterranean coast was inhabited first by Neanderthals and then Homo sapiens, but the continuity of tools and personal objects suggests there was some sharing of culture between the two species

new-sci.title: How healthy is your brain? We now know how to find out
new-sci.description: In our efforts to keep our brains healthy, how do we know what is working? Helen Thomson explores a new generation of tests that can reveal whether our efforts are paying off

new-sci.title: 5 things to know about sunscreen, according to a skin cancer expert
new-sci.description: How much sunscreen should you be using, when should you apply it, and are there any downsides to doing so? Skin cancer expert Rachel Neale is here to answer all of these questions and more

new-sci.title: Musical take on The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind is moving and charming
new-sci.description: A TED talk and then a film, William Kamkwamba’s story of how he worked to provide his rural Malawian village with electricity has now been turned into a musical – and it mostly works, says Bethan Ackerley

new-sci.title: Collapse of AMOC ocean current may already be locked in
new-sci.description: The fate of the Atlantic Ocean current that keeps Europe’s climate warm depends on our carbon emissions and the rate of ice melt from Greenland, but there is a chance that a shutdown is already inevitable

new-sci.title: Human brains may have got bigger for no particular reason
new-sci.description: Our brains are large compared with other animals, so it is tempting to assume there was an evolutionary advantage to them – but that may not be true at all

new-sci.title: Beetroot juice is trending – its benefits go beyond the hype
new-sci.description: Some marathon runners and other athletes swear by beetroot juice shots, but is there evidence they really do anything for our bodies? Columnist Alice Klein investigates

new-sci.title: Can the biggest problems in AI be solved by philosophy?
new-sci.description: AI companies are hiring philosophy graduates to help them understand the nature of consciousness, whether it can be replicated and how their systems can be made better and more reliable

new-sci.title: ‘Hobbit’ hominins scavenged meat left over by Komodo dragons
new-sci.description: An experiment that involved feeding a dead goat to a Komodo dragon as well as an analysis of thousands of ancient bones suggests that Homo floresiensis was neither a skilled hunter of big game nor a master of fire

new-sci.title: A volcano has erupted remnants of Earth's primordial magma ocean
new-sci.description: Earth was once covered by a global magma ocean, which later cooled and crystallised – now traces of this primordial event have been found in magma from a young volcano in the Indian Ocean

new-sci.title: Audacious mission to rescue NASA's falling telescope has launched
new-sci.description: NASA’s Swift space telescope is reaching the end of its two-decade run in orbit – unless a satellite launched on 3 July can give it a lifesaving boost

new-sci.title: Orangutan mothers seem to plan playdates for their offspring
new-sci.description: Female orangutans are generally solitary, but they travel more and eat less in an apparent effort to ensure their offspring have someone to play with

new-sci.title: This thoughtful book will make you look at the wonders of trees anew
new-sci.description: Aya Koda's Tree is an account of the late writer's visits to Japan's most famous, and ancient, trees. Featured in Wim Wenders's film Perfect Days, it is original and thought-provoking, says Rowan Hooper

new-sci.title: Stunning photos reveal the intricate beauty of fungi
new-sci.description: The vibrant colours and delicate details of New Zealand's fungi and slime moulds are documented in these images, taken from Jay Lichter's new book The Secret Life of Fungi

new-sci.title: Evocative photos of Canadian Arctic win New Scientist Editors Award
new-sci.description: Natalya Saprunova's photo series exploring coastal erosion and permafrost thaw across Inuvialuit territories in Canada has won the New Scientist Editors Award at the Earth Photo 2026 competition

undark.title: Biologists Should Articulate Their Position on AI
undark.description: Last month, mathematics researchers released the Leiden Declaration, a treatise on how to handle the challenges that artificial intelligence poses to their field. C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that biologists should learn from the mathematics community and work on their own version.

undark.title: Review: What Animals Can Teach Humans About Caregiving
undark.description: From seahorses and birds to beetles and killer whales, journalist Elizabeth Preston finds a lot of common ground  between human and animal parenting in “The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” a sweeping survey of the evolution of caregiving and the dizzying array of survival strategies in the animal kingdom.

undark.title: The MAHA Movement’s Worrisome Embrace of Ibogaine
undark.description: The MAHA movement has been promoting the plant-based substance ibogaine as a remedy for opioid addiction, despite the lack of clinical trials on its safety and efficacy. One physician who practices addiction medicine discusses the risks of ibogaine and argues for the need to support proven treatments.

undark.title: Advocacy Groups Express Mixed Views on Embryo Editing
undark.description: At least two new start-up companies, Preventive and Origin Genomics, say they are developing strategies that combine gene editing with in vitro fertilization to correct disease-causing mutations. Advocacy groups for people living with these genetic disorders have been quiet on the developments.

undark.title: Interview: California Lawmaker Calls for a Peptide Working Group
undark.description: Amid a national push to ease restrictions on certain peptides, California legislator Joe Patterson has introduced a state-level bill that would to establish a working group tasked with making recommendations to allow physicians and hospitals, among others, to prescribe and study promising peptides.

undark.title: Making Sense of Data From Wearable Health Trackers
undark.description: Wearable health devices such as smartwatches, glucose monitors, and sleep trackers are blurring the line between consumer wellness and clinical medicine. One physician argues that validation standards and privacy protections must be established to ensure the usefulness of the data these devices generate.

undark.title: In California, a Plan to Help Wildlife Cross a Busy Freeway
undark.description: The 101 freeway in California bisects a mountainous region where threatened cougars and other animals are blocked without a viable path across 10 lanes of heavily trafficked roadway. But an ambitious 210-foot “vegetated bridge” will soon be home to what organizers say is the largest wildlife crossing anywhere in the world.

undark.title: Promising ‘Liquid Biopsies’ May Not Be Ready for Primetime
undark.description: Multi-cancer early detection tests seek to spot cancer from a single blood draw. Enabling earlier cancer diagnoses could help save lives and limit the need for invasive interventions. But while the tests are promising, physicians have expressed doubt about routine use by low-risk and asymptomatic individuals.

undark.title: Book Review: How Radio Astronomy Made the Invisible Visible
undark.description: According to astronomer Emma Chapman’s revelatory “The Echoing Universe,” the history of radio astronomy is filled with surprises that have revealed parts of the universe that would otherwise remain hidden and invisible — DIY instruments, secrets accidentally uncovered, and persistent connections to Earth.

undark.title: Risk Aversion in Science Stifles Innovation
undark.description: Does the scientific enterprise play it too safe? C. Brandon Ogbunu argues that risk-taking in science involves a willingness to reflect on the processes and incentives of the profession — and to dramatically overhaul them if they do not work. Only then can true scientific innovation take shape.

proj-syn.title: Inside Ukraine’s Game-Changing Drone Industry
proj-syn.description: In recent months, Ukrainian drones have successfully struck dozens of sites deep inside Russia, targeting the oil industry, weapons plants, and logistics hubs. But while Ukraine has developed a world-leading military technology to defend itself from a much larger aggressor, drones will not be enough to end the war.

proj-syn.title: Just Say No to Remote Work
proj-syn.description: Even during the immediate post-pandemic period, when evidence on the labor-market effects of remote work was scant, there was a strong case to be made for going into the office, especially for younger workers. And now, multiple new studies have vindicated this intuition.

proj-syn.title: There Is Only One Acceptable Path for Designer Babies
proj-syn.description: Genetic-engineering tools with which to design one's progeny already exist, and they are being made even more potent with AI—at least for those who can afford such services. In the absence of policy interventions, we will be hurtling toward a tiered society in which economic privileges become biological advantages.

proj-syn.title: The Democratic Turkey NATO Needs
proj-syn.description: At NATO's upcoming summit in Ankara, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan will seek to portray his country as stable, confident, and essential to Western security. But only the last one is true, which is why the restoration of democracy in Turkey is more than a domestic concern.

proj-syn.title: The World Cup as It Should Be
proj-syn.description: While Donald Trump was widely expected to lord over this year’s World Cup, which the United States is co-hosting with Mexico and Canada, it has turned out not to be his scene. National teams populated with immigrants, and small-town America’s embrace of the event, go against everything Trump’s MAGA movement stands for.

proj-syn.title: The Real Threat to NATO
proj-syn.description: The greatest challenge to NATO comes not from its adversaries but from within. As its leaders gather in Ankara on July 7-8, they should focus less on military capabilities than on reinvigorating the alliance's founding strategic philosophy, centered on democratic legitimacy, human rights, and the rule of law.

proj-syn.title: How the EU Can Lead the Rest of the West
proj-syn.description: While Europe is not just another middle power, nor is it a great power with sufficient economic, military, and geopolitical clout to dictate terms on the global stage. Instead, Europe is the ideal candidate to convene and lead a group of like-minded middle powers, not as a US-style hegemon, but as a first among equals.

proj-syn.title: Europe Must Face the World on Its Own
proj-syn.description: Under pressure from Russian aggression—which has reached its full expression in the ongoing war against Ukraine—and an increasingly hostile US administration, Europe urgently needs to make progress toward a defense union. But that will require Franco-German leadership of the kind that is not yet on offer.

proj-syn.title: How Safe Are Today’s Blockbuster Tech Stocks?
proj-syn.description: Today’s wave of mega-IPOs has unleashed a wave of analogies to past booms. While no analogy is perfect, an especially apposite—and sobering—case may be what followed Nippon Telegraph and Telephone’s IPO in February 1987.

proj-syn.title: Europe’s AI Dolce Vita?
proj-syn.description: Glacial growth, aging welfare states, and a shortage of centrist leaders suggest Europe faces a major debt crisis in the years ahead. But its emphasis on leisure over work could become a decisive advantage, positioning the continent as the leading model for thriving in an age of AI-driven abundance.

proj-syn.title: The Putin Escalation Risk
proj-syn.description: If Ukraine can continue to disrupt Crimea, strike more targets in the heart of Russia, frustrate Russia’s frontline forces, and pile more pressure on Russia’s hobbled economy, President Vladimir Putin will feel increasingly cornered. The temptation to escape his predicament through a game-changing attack will grow stronger.

proj-syn.title: Europe’s New German Question
proj-syn.description: Without a EU-level framework capable of turning resources into scale, the bloc’s defense capabilities will remain limited, no matter how much member countries spends. If Germany, in particular, insists on going it alone, Europe could remain fully dependent on the US for key assets.

proj-syn.title: From the American Revolution to Universal Suffrage
proj-syn.description: Britain’s attempt to crush the American Revolution exposed a constitutional crisis at the heart of its empire. One English statesman saw in it proof that only broader suffrage could check royal power, tame corruption, and ensure that imperial rule remained compatible with liberty.

proj-syn.title: 250 Years of American State Capitalism
proj-syn.description: While the prevailing economic narrative in the United States has often extolled free markets, policymaking itself has always been more pragmatic. From its very founding, the US has had a hybrid model in which the state directs, subsidizes, and occasionally bails out private enterprise in the service of national priorities.

proj-syn.title: Three Essentials of a More Equal World Order
proj-syn.description: A growing awareness of the inequities embedded in the world order has prompted calls for reform. Building a multilateral system that serves the global majority will require redesigning the international financial architecture, especially in relation to sovereign debt and corporate taxation.

proj-syn.title: The US as the World’s Robber Baron
proj-syn.description: Like the Gilded Age robber barons, the United States under President Donald Trump is using trade policy to benefit itself at the expense of all other countries. But now that administration surrogates are openly acknowledging the strategy, all other major trading powers will surely respond accordingly.

proj-syn.title: A Democratic Opening for Azerbaijan
proj-syn.description: With Armenia's recent elections likely to usher in an era of greater stability—and less Russian influence—in the South Caucasus, neighboring Azerbaijan is well-positioned to deepen cooperation with the US and Europe. But without appropriate conditions, new strategic partnerships with the West could fail to deliver for Azerbaijanis.

proj-syn.title: The Mismeasure of Europe’s Economy
proj-syn.description: While Nobel laureate economists Paul Krugman and Philippe Aghion disagree over how to measure Europe’s productivity gap with the United States, both overlook the value of its accumulated assets. That blind spot obscures the real story: Europe is living off a remarkable inheritance it has yet to convert into new growth.
